told_more: The record gave every event with its date and cause (who, why, in what order), and covers things a picture cannot carry: repaints, shop closures, who lived or traded where, the 1935 fire and rebuild, why a house was empty. The views are in plain grey-yellow clay with no paint colour, signs or people, so they show only the events that changed geometry: shopfronts going in and out (A, B), the balcony (B), window changes (C gable and back wall, D), boards going up and coming down (D, E). Even those I could only date by matching them to the record. The views did add something: where each house sits, how far each change reads at eye level, street, 12 m and city scale, and the extent of some additions. They confirmed the record more than they taught me new history.

contradicts.claim: B reads as a low-pitched roof with ribbed grey cladding in the city and 12 m views, rather than the flat roof the record gives for the 1936 functionalist house; from the quay only the flat parapet edge shows. Possibly a flat roof drawn with a slope, but it looks pitched from above.

B's bakery shopfront (2000, 2010, 2020) is a solid blank panel under a plain fascia, with a blank dark box above the door and no glazed display window. It reads as shuttered or boarded, not as an open bakery; nothing in the record says the bakery closed.
E in 2000 looks exactly like E in 1989: windows glazed, nothing let go, although the record says it was left empty and neglected from 1993. Neglect before the 2008 boarding is not shown.

D in 1989 and 2000 shows boarded windows but otherwise sound walls, trim and roof, although the record says it stood empty for 21 years and the roof let in water by 1995. The views understate how neglected it was.

B's balcony in 2010 and 2020 sits over a fully glazed ground-floor annex (a ribbed glass veranda or sunroom along the lane wall) that the record does not mention; the record has only a balcony over the lane.

A has a bay window (oriel) on the upper left, with a smaller window under it, in every year and view. The record does not list it as a feature or as an event, so I read it as part of the 1912 house but cannot confirm this.
A's shopfront looks the same in 2010 as in 2000, with no sign of the 2009 closure.

views_showed: Where things are: A and B face each other across the foot of the lane; C and D flank the landing, with D high on its rock outcrop; E, small and dark, closes the view at the top. D and E are the two houses that dominate the view up the lane, so their boards (D until 2007, E from 2008) are the strongest signal in the street and 12 m views.

Boarding reads instantly at every scale. D's boards in 1989 and 2000 and their removal in 2007 (framed nine-pane windows) are plain in the street and 12 m views. E goes from open windows to boarded between 2000 and 2010 and shows that even in the city view.

How big the changes are: B's 1997 shopfront and 2003 balcony (with the glazed annex below it) and A's 2016 shopfront removal (the ground floor gets three windows and a door again, matching the upper rhythm) are visible at eye level and partly from the city view. They are the largest changes on the corner.

C's changes are small and local. The 1998 copies show only in the upper window of the gable end. The 1971 plain louvred windows stay on the ground floor. The 2011 factory windows with heavy surrounds show on the back wall, so the wall ends up with mixed generations of windows.
D's lean-to at the back is visible from 12 m in every year, which fits its 1950 date.

Which view shows which house: the eye view only A and B; the street view C, D and E; the 12 m view C, D and E with boards and windows; the city view little more than B's balcony and annex, A's ground floor and E's boards.
missing: All repaints (A 1949/1996/2016, B 1987/2003/2017, C 1998/2013, D 2007): no paint colour or weathering shows, so who painted and when is invisible.
Every cause and actor: the cannery owner, widow, heirs in Oslo, young family, break-in, the oil-price fall, the city's wooden-town rules. None can be seen.
The businesses: Vik Jernvare, Kaffebrenneriet and Quay Bakery have no readable signs, goods or people. A's café and the 2009 closure leave no trace in the views.
B's 1884 chalet house, its 1935 fire and the 1936 rebuild: only the current functionalist house is shown, and I could not tell it from its clapboard neighbours by style.
Architectural styles (jugend, Swiss chalet, empire, functionalist): C, D and E look like plain clapboard gable houses; only A's mansard roof stands out.
The 1965 front-window replacements on D and E: nothing identifies them as newer than the walls.
E's neglect from 1993 to 2008 and the 2015 'still empty': E looks identical in 1989 and 2000, and unchanged from 2010 to 2020.
D's roof leak and neglected condition from 1986 to 2007: only the boards show, and D's roof looks intact.
The doors boarded up on D and E: I could not see the doors in the views, only windows.
Which windows are copies: A's 2016 windows (copies of the 1912 ones), C's 1998 windows and D's 2007 windows look like ordinary old-style windows, so a viewer cannot tell copies from originals.
